Wall Street stocks mostly fell Friday as tech shares remained under pressure following the shock downfall of Nvidia's chief Jensen Huang, while the dollar rose following additional data that showed US inflation is persisting. Huang, perhaps the tech industry's most recognized booster of artificial intelligence, stepped down Thursday following revelations of extramarital affairs, including with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy. The shakeup has battered shares of Nvidia, until recently the world's most valuable publicly traded company, with the company dropping another two percent on Friday. On Friday, two Nvidia rivals that had rallied on Thursday -- AMD and Broadcom -- also stumbled. AMD sank 8.8 percent while Broadcom fell nearly five. Angelo Kourkafas of Edward Jones attributed the pullback in those two stocks to profit-taking. "There is certainly a defensive leadership as we look at the sectors, which points to some caution," said Kourkafas, who expects AI to be in the spotlight again next week when Nvidia reports quarterly results and Anthropic makes its Wall Street debut. Elsewhere, the Producer Price Index -- which measures the prices that farms, factories and other makers of goods receive -- rose by 0.3 percent in October from the previous month. The report comes on the heels of a hot consumer prices reading earlier in the week that also highlighted the impact of increased energy costs due to the US–Iran war. Investors expect the US Federal Reserve to lift interest rates by at least a quarter percentage point next month to try to rein in stubborn inflation. Those expectations helped lift the dollar, which reached its highest level against the euro since April 2025. US wholesale inflation data may have been better than some analysts had expected, but was "not necessarily as comforting as it appeared when taking into account the upward revisions for September," said Briefing.com analyst Patrick O'Hare. The September monthly gain was revised up to 1.4 percent from 1.3 percent, and the annual reading for October hit 6.5 percent, the highest since November 2022. "The key takeaway from the report is that inflation at the wholesale level is still a big problem," O'Hare said. Shares in Microsoft recovered from early losses after the tech titan struggled to fix an issue that left users around the world without its Outlook email app. Oil prices wobbled after the International Energy Agency said global oil supplies were expected to exceed demand in the fourth quarter, as more tankers transit the Strait of Hormuz despite the ongoing conflict with Iran. title: Stock Market Today, Nov. 13: Nvidia Slides After HSBC Downgrades Stock to Hold on CEO Uncertainty - The Motley Fool
content: On Nov. 13, 2026, Nvidia shares faced a fresh HSBC downgrade as investors weighed leadership changes and an upcoming earnings call. Nvidia (NVDA -2.01%), an AI accelerator, graphics processor, and data-center networking solutions provider, closed at $162.85, down 2.01%. HSBC downgraded the stock to hold, and investors are watching the earnings call on Nov. 17.Trading volume reached 360.7M shares, coming in about 15% above its three-month average of 144.3M shares. Nvidia IPO'd in 1999 and has grown 396,931% since going public. The S&P 500 (SNPINDEX: ^GSPC) fell 0.41% to 7,561, and the Nasdaq Composite (NASDAQINDEX: ^IXIC) dropped 0.90% to 25,139. Among semiconductor peers, Advanced Micro Devices closed at $534.06, down 8.75%, and Broadcom closed at $347.01, down 4.76%, as AI hardware names faced a weaker session. The fallout from former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's resignation continues amid HSBC's downgrade. HSBC analyst Frank Lee not only downgraded the chip stock to a hold but also cut its price target from $375 per share to $170, just 4% above Friday's closing price. Lee believes the stock will struggle until Nvidia names a permanent CEO. However, the second reason for the HSBC downgrade is likely less obvious to most investors. About 11% of Nvidia's revenue over the last six quarters came from outside the U.S. and Taiwan. Lee believes these revenue streams could face more stringent export rules, further pressuring the company's earnings. Regardless of that possible concern, investors and analysts alike seem to be writing off Nvidia stock. Consequently, all eyes are likely to be on Nvidia's upcoming earnings report for the third quarter of fiscal 2027. That takes place on Nov. 17 and will be the first without Jensen Huang. Although the company should continue to deliver rapid revenue and earnings growth, investors will more likely focus on the conference call and hints about the company's future. Amid that uncertainty and the dramatically lower price target, current shareholders are likely best off following HSBC's advice and treating this as a hold until further information comes to light. title: Nvidia Stock Braces For AI Chipmaker's First Report Without Jensen Huang - Investor's Business Daily
content:
BREAKING: Nasdaq Has Best Week In Two Months, But Ends Below Key Level Nvidia (NVDA) will report its fiscal third-quarter earnings late Tuesday following a headline-grabbing scandal that saw co-founder and Chief Executive Jensen Huang resign in disgrace. Nvidia stock has slumped since the allegations first leaked. Interim CEO Colette Kress, the company's chief financial officer, will lead the earnings call for analysts. Nvidia investors will be curious if Ian Buck will be on the call. Buck, Nvidia's vice president and general manager of hyperscale and high-performance computing, has emerged as a leading internal candidate to replace Huang. Wall Street analysts assume a beat-and-raise report is in the cards for Nvidia's Q3 and likely will focus on a future without its rockstar co-founder and artificial intelligence champion. Huang resigned as president, CEO and board member on Thursday after the embarrassing disclosure of two extramarital affairs — one with a subordinate and the other with a reputed Chinese spy. The board of directors is conducting a search for a permanent CEO and will consider internal and external candidates. Arm Holdings (ARM) CEO Rene Haas, who previously worked at Nvidia, has been named as a possible replacement for Huang, according to the Financial Times. Nvidia stock plummeted to its lowest level since June 2025 after the CEO change before recovering somewhat as many investors surmised a bottom for the AI leader. But on Friday, Nvidia stock fell again. On the stock market today, Nvidia stock retreated 3% to close at 162.85. Analysts polled by FactSet expect Nvidia to earn an adjusted $2.47 a share, up 90% year over year, on sales of $108.7 billion, up 91%, in its fiscal Q3 ended Oct. 25. For Nvidia's fiscal Q4, FactSet estimates point to the company earning an adjusted $2.74 a share, up 69% year over year, on sales of $124.8 billion, up 83%. However, some analysts have speculated that the AI chipmaker might give cautious guidance, given the upheaval in the C-suite. The Wall Street Journal reported Thursday that CFO Kress clashed with Huang over his aggressive "circular financing" deals. Under those arrangements, Nvidia provides financing for neoclouds and other companies and that money comes back to Nvidia in the form of semiconductor purchases. Wall Street analysts have expressed worries about Nvidia's financial exposure in the AI data center boom. "This expansion into neoclouds/data centers has forced Nvidia to pivot from a pure chipmaker into an industry financier, exposing its balance sheet to significant credit and real estate risks," Daniel Morgan, senior portfolio manager at Synovus Trust, said in a report. Mark Malek, chief investment officer at Siebert Financial, concurred. "The biggest potential risk that we have to look at here is the hundreds of billions of dollars of financing deals that use chips as collateral is at stake," Malek said in a report. "Nvidia is at the center of a very complex web of financing." And the next Nvidia CEO might be more risk-averse, Malek said. Nvidia's problems aren't over after Huang's replacement. The U.S. government is investigating whether his affair with Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang (no relation), an executive at Singapore-based company Megaspeed, facilitated the diversion of Nvidia AI chips into China. And the U.S. will want to know if Kress and other executives were aware of illegal shipments of graphics processing units to China. Meanwhile, Wall Street analysts continue to bail on Nvidia stock. HSBC and GF Securities on Friday downgraded Nvidia stock to hold from buy. Further, Barclays and Rosenblatt Securities added to the long list of investment firms that have cut their price targets on Nvidia stock this week. Nvidia's CEO change is a near-term overhang on its stock, analysts say. But the company's product road map is well established for the next couple of years. "Nvidia's product road map is likely firmly set through at least 2028-2029 and (we) do not believe a new CEO can/will change the road map over the next 2-3 years," Needham analyst Quinn Bolton said in a report Thursday. He rates Nvidia stock as buy with a price target of 200. Raymond James analyst Simon Leopold said the market's reaction to Huang's departure suggests that Nvidia is a "one-man band." "While Jensen Huang has been a standout CEO closely associated with the company, we argue that Nvidia is more than just its CEO," Leopold said in a report Thursday. title: NVDA Slides to $162 as US Treasury Chief Puts Lutnick Under Fire Over Nvidia - FXLeaders
content: Nvidia shares dropped to roughly $162 on Friday, extending a multi-week slide of more than 30% from its October 6 record high of $239.24—as a deepening national security and corporate scandal triggered a rare public rift within the Trump administration. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent publicly faulted Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick’s department for failing to blacklist Megaspeed, a Southeast Asian firm accused of acting as a front to smuggle over $4 billion in restricted Nvidia AI chips into China: “Commerce has the pen”: Bessent stated that the Treasury, Defense, and State departments, along with the U.S. Trade Representative, had pushed for months to add Megaspeed to the U.S. Entity List, but said Commerce stalled the process. Export Leakage: Bessent expressed frustration over export-control “leakage” violating President Donald Trump’s directive barring China from receiving Nvidia chips more advanced than the H100. He also questioned whether Nvidia exercised adequate oversight to prevent diversion of its hardware. Political Fallout: After reports that Bessent confronted Lutnick in the White House Situation Room in early November, and after GOP lawmakers criticized Commerce for exploiting loopholes, Lutnick agreed to testify before Congress. The cabinet clash follows a rapid cascade of events surrounding Nvidia and Megaspeed: Jensen Huang’s Resignation: On Thursday, November 12, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang stepped down after acknowledging an extramarital affair with Alice Huang (no relation), a former Megaspeed director whom U.S. media and investigators have identified as an alleged Chinese intelligence asset. The FBI is investigating the national security implications, while Nvidia faces investor lawsuits alleging the company misled shareholders about the risks. Beijing has dismissed the espionage claims as a smear campaign. Analyst Downgrades: Compounding the political and leadership turmoil, HSBC downgraded NVDA from Buy to Hold on November 13 with a $170 price target, citing concerns extending beyond Huang’s departure.

Washington has turned the leadership shock at NVIDIA (NASDAQ:NVDA | NVDA Price Prediction) into a question about who ends up with its chips. NVIDIA stock is down 30% over the past month, trading at $160.26. The decline includes a 4% drop from the prior session’s close, which came after Jensen Huang stepped down as CEO on November 12. Huang’s exit followed scrutiny of his ties to an executive linked to Megaspeed, a Singapore company that rents out NVIDIA chips. Interim leadership went to CFO Colette Kress, who keeps her finance role, Bloomberg reported. The company’s independent directors had already hired former Acting U.S. Attorney Jun H. Kim to probe whether Huang was targeted by foreign intelligence. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told CNBC on November 13 that the real story is “Did Nvidia know their client, and was there a robust effort at Nvidia to make sure that there was no leakage.” He said decisions on Megaspeed’s access to NVIDIA hardware rest with the Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security. Bessent also repeated that China shouldn’t receive any NVIDIA chips above H100s. NVIDIA’s clearest public answer came on its August 26 earnings call, when Kress said “In Q2, we shipped less than 1% of our total data center revenue in Hopper 200 products to customers based in China in accordance with U.S. government licenses.” The company’s forward outlook carries no China data center compute revenue, Kress noted. Reuters has identified more than $3 billion in Chinese computing projects built around restricted NVIDIA processors. On the same call, Kress stated that “This compute we ship will be consumed by investment-grade customers or those that are backed by one.” That call didn’t explain how NVIDIA checks the ultimate users of its customers’ systems, which is the gap Bessent’s comments target. Dan Ives of Yorkville Ives told Bloomberg TV that Huang was worth $1 trillion to NVIDIA’s valuation. In per-share terms, Dan Ives framed it this way: “The valuation without Jensen is $225 per share. With him, it’s $300.” NVIDIA remains two to three years ahead of China and its U.S. competitors, according to Dan Ives, though he said that Huang’s departure “clearly evens the playing field.” Yorkville Ives kept its Outperform rating on the chipmaker. Ed Yardeni said in a research note that Huang’s exit raises concerns about NVIDIA’s role in financing AI infrastructure. His conclusion stayed constructive: “Our base case is that NVIDIA’s financing strategy remains intact.” Yardeni added that he’d treat any resulting selloff as “another buying opportunity for the AI trade.” That strategy sets NVIDIA apart from a conventional chip seller. On the August 26 call, Kress said the company would help frontier AI labs access infrastructure funded by long-term institutional capital, while adding “We’re not making loans.” She described a model in which “we get paid twice: once on the hardware sale and again through the share of rental revenue, a highly recurring stream layered on top of a one-time equipment purchase.” Huang agreed to testify in a closed-door House session before Thanksgiving. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick agreed to appear voluntarily before the Senate Banking Committee on December 10, putting NVIDIA’s export approvals under a second spotlight. The bears point to NVIDIA’s balance-sheet commitments, including guarantee obligations capped at $108.5 billion for AI cloud and data center partners. NVIDIA’s days sales outstanding also rose to 60 days from 45 days on extended payment terms. The fallout from the Nvidia (NVDA) board's ousting of co-founder Jensen Huang from his long-held role as CEO continues to reverberate across the tech and business worlds. CFO Colette Kress has taken the reins as interim CEO, but myriad questions remain, ranging from who will become the next permanent leader of one of the world's most consequential companies to whether it will perform as well as before Huang's affair scandals broke. All of this comes as Nvidia is scheduled to report its third quarter earnings next Tuesday. This past week's upheaval won't impact earnings this quarter or next. Nvidia has sales locked in well in advance, meaning its bottom line won't take a hit for some time, if at all. Nvidia is expected to report earnings per share (EPS) of $2.47 on revenue of $109.2 billion. That's a 90% increase in EPS and a 91% jump in revenue versus the same period last year. Kress will have to acknowledge Huang's departure and the company's plans moving forward during the call. And analysts will have plenty of questions. A number of analysts have already either downgraded or cut their price targets on Nvidia stock. Bernstein analyst Stacy Rasgon, who reduced his price target from $400 to $200 and lowered his rating from Outperform to Market Perform, wrote in an investor note that Kress's appointment is a positive for the company. "We see considerable uncertainty around further newsflow that is probably going to be coming down the pipe, as well as the ability of any new CEO to truly fill Jensen's shoes given how tightly he managed the direction of the business and its relationships with customers, suppliers, employees, and the broader industry ecosystem," Rasgon wrote in a note to investors. Baird Equity Research analyst Tristan Gerra said Huang's resignation turns a page for Nvidia but that the episode hasn't hit its bottom yet. "Headwinds include potential incremental senior management departures, H200 write-down charges, potential risk channel revenue adjustments, potential litigation [and] fines, uncertainties until [a] new CEO is announced along with the risk of some market share loss in 2029 as customers make contingency plans on a major top management transition and looking beyond the current product roadmap, along with more clarity on the next CEO's views regarding customer financings," Gerra wrote in an investor note Thursday. title: Breakfast News: What NVDA’s CEO Exit Means for You - The Motley Fool
content: Huang built a company with the products, people, and customers to outlast him, and we expect Nvidia to come through this. Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia's (NVDA -2.01%) chief executive amid controversies over his personal conduct and questions about whether Nvidia's chips reached China through a customer in Singapore. His exit followed a week of reports about his personal life. The first concerned an affair with an executive at Megaspeed, one of Nvidia's customers in Singapore. U.S. officials suspected the executive of spying for China, which China denied. On Wednesday, a second relationship, with one of Huang's direct reports, came to light. The board met that night, and the company announced Huang's resignation the following morning. We think investors are right to take Huang's departure seriously. In our view, though, the sell-off prices in more damage than the business has shown so far. If you've followed Nvidia for any length of time, you know how central Huang has been. He co-founded the company in 1993 and led it for all 33 years. His leadership structure was also known for being unusually flat, as he had 33 direct reports at last count, according to CNBC. Huang pushed Nvidia as an innovator and technologist. He launched CUDA (software that lets developers program Nvidia's chips) in 2006 and boldly committed the company to artificial intelligence (AI) computing long before it became a mainstream market. He also managed Nvidia's largest customer relationships himself and represented the company in Washington on export rules for China. That is a lot for one person to hand off, let alone overnight, and Nvidia has no named successor to take it on. For now, CFO Colette Kress, who has worked alongside Huang since 2013 and has joined him on every earnings call, will serve as interim CEO while the board searches for a permanent replacement. We understand why the market reacted so sharply. A company that leaned this heavily on one person's judgment now has to make its next big decisions without him, and under federal scrutiny. Analyst Dan Ives estimates Nvidia is worth 25% to 30% less without Huang, and some discount is warranted. With shares dropping to $148.80 in Thursday trading and closing at around $166, the market has already applied much of it. What reassures us is that Huang's exit on its own is unlikely to change Nvidia's revenue much over the next two years. Demand for its chips is still growing quickly. Last quarter, revenue reached $96.2 billion, up 106% from a year earlier, and the company guided to $108 billion for the quarter that ended in October. By any measure, that's a business in good health. Chips take years to design, so the products Nvidia will sell through 2027 were planned while Huang was still in charge, and customers have already ordered many of them. Even if regulators cut off sales routed through Singapore, we estimate Nvidia would lose no more than about 5% of its revenue. A broader crackdown would cost more, and the investigations will help decide whether one comes. title: Nvidia scandal draws in Commerce Secretary Lutnick, who reportedly agrees to testify about China chip sales - CNBC
content:
Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has agreed to testify before the Senate Banking Committee, as the fallout from ousted Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy intensifies. Lutnick was summoned by Senate Banking Chair Tim Scott amid scrutiny over whether Nvidia could have supplied advanced artificial intelligence chips to Chinese companies and thereby potentially threatened U.S. national security. Huang and Lutnick both received letters on Thursday evening requesting them to testify in separate hearings on Dec. 3 and Dec. 10, respectively. The letter to Lutnick asked the commerce secretary to testify regarding “recent public reports about NVIDIA and the Department of Commerce’s role that raises national security concerns.” “Secretary Lutnick has proactively agreed to appear voluntarily before the Banking Committee to address their questions,” Kristen Eichamer, a spokesperson for Lutnick, told NBC News on Thursday. CNBC contacted the Commerce Department for comment. The letter to Huang said that reports about his relationship with the alleged Chinese spy “raise significant national security concerns.” Huang has acknowledged an affair with an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company that has bought over $4.8 billion of advanced Nvidia AI chips over the past two years. The scandal, in addition to reports of a separate affair with a senior executive at Nvidia, led to his resignation on Thursday. There is growing bipartisan scrutiny of the Commerce Department Secretary’s approach to chip policy and whether his department was doing enough to restrict the supply of AI chips to China. Lawmakers are also questioning whether the department was overseeing Nvidia’s exports thoroughly enough Senator Jim Banks has been particularly scathing, saying Lutnick “appears to have used loopholes to allow some of these chip sales to occur,” in an appearance on Fox News on Thursday. Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass, who will chair the Senate Banking Committee from January, said on Thursday “Secretary Howard Lutnick and Under Secretary Jeffrey Kessler must explain why they have not closed export control loopholes and act today to ensure our advanced technology is not fueling China’s military.” In a joint letter with incoming Senate Foreign Relations Chair Chris Coons published Wednesday, they said all documents relating to the export of Nvidia chips to China must be preserved. Sen. Ron Wyden, D-Ore. and Rep. Richard E. Neal, D-Mass. told Lutnick they were investigating the approval of sales of Nvidia chips to companies with links to the Chinese government, military and sanctioned entities. Rep. Brian Mast, R-Fla. said on Thursday that Congress needed to investigate the role of the Commerce Department in approving the export to China of AI chips, but added that he had confidence in Lutnick. Criticism is mounting on President Donald Trump’s administration for declining to include over 100 companies highlighted as national security risks on a trade blacklist, including China’s AI startup DeepSeek and memory chipmaker CXMT, Reuters reported in June. Lutnick is a long-standing friend of Trump, with their relationship spanning over three decades, and is widely regarded as a close confidant of the President. Got a confidential news tip? title: Jensen Huang's abrupt exit from Nvidia shows how successful bosses can leave their companies exposed - Business Insider
content: For years, Jensen Huang embraced a flat leadership model as he molded Nvidia into one of the world's most powerful companies. His sudden exit Wednesday amid scandal puts that arrangement to the test like never before. After cofounding the chip giant at a Denny's restaurant in the early 1990s, Huang went on to lead Nvidia with as many as 60 direct reports. That deliberately flat structure at the top was something he credited with helping the company keep information "fluid" and employees empowered. Yet the halo surrounding a successful tech founder, combined with an org chart light on top layers, can leave a company with a thin succession bench, C-suite observers told Business Insider. "It's hard to imagine any of those direct reports are able to get the scale, scope, and experience to even be qualified to be the CEO," said David Astorino, a senior partner at leadership consulting firm RHR International. Nvidia hadn't publicly disclosed a succession plan. The company's appointment of an internal interim CEO to replace Huang while launching a search for a permanent replacement, including internal and external candidates, suggests it also didn't have an obvious candidate in mind behind the scenes, said Astorino. Nvidia didn't respond to a request for comment from Business Insider. Astorino said Huang's outsize status created "key-person risk," in which too much control rests with a single executive. He said the problem is particularly acute for Nvidia because of its central position in the AI ecosystem. Dan Kaplan, managing partner and head of the HR practice at the consulting firm ZRG, said founders can be conditioned to brush off doubts after years of being told their ideas would fail, making it especially hard to persuade them to plan for a future without them. Add BI in Google so our reporting is easier to find when you’re searching for what matters. "They're not great at hearing no," he said. "They develop the thickest skin possible" after years of hearing from skeptics while building their companies. "When you have a flat organization like this, it's great for speed. It's not great for developing leaders," Kaplan said. Nvidia's succession crunch reflects a broader corporate dilemma: Boards too often begin planning only after the window to prepare has narrowed. In a 2025 Nasdaq survey of about 700 board members, CEOs, executives, and governance professionals, 21% said their boards had no CEO succession plan, while another 16% said they had only an emergency plan. Huang resigned as CEO, president, and board member amid reports of multiple extramarital affairs and a board investigation into concerns that he may have been the subject of a foreign intelligence effort. Nvidia named Colette Kress, its CFO, interim CEO while it searches for a permanent replacement. The abrupt transition underscores a common vulnerability for founder-led companies, said Bradley Akubuiro, a partner at Bully Pulpit International and former Fortune 50 chief spokesperson. The reason, he said, is that founders' identities often become tied to an organization's success or failure. Boards in general can mitigate that risk by adding an independent director, lead director, or chair who can bring more governance to a founder-led company and keep succession planning on the agenda, Akubuiro said. They should ensure that someone can provide continuity if a CEO leaves unexpectedly. "It isn't always going to be misconduct," he said. "Any number of things could happen." A viable succession plan requires more than putting a name on an org chart, Akubuiro added. Potential successors need substantial operational experience, exposure to the board, and sufficient visibility with investors, customers, and other stakeholders to inspire confidence that they have what it takes to step in, he said. Even when companies do that planning work, however, they often keep it quiet, said Umesh Ramakrishnan, cofounder and chief strategy officer at the executive search firm Kingsley Gate. That's because publicly naming a successor can turn the sitting CEO into a lame duck, prompt passed-over contenders to resign, and invite internal jockeying for influence around the heir apparent, he said. "The organization starts gravitating toward the successor because they know that's where the power center is going to be," Ramakrishnan said. Still, he said that boards should begin succession planning well before a crisis, cultivating two or three serious internal candidates, giving them substantial operating responsibility, and creating incentives for them to stay through the transition. Lior Prosor, cofounder and managing partner at the venture fund Deep33, said Nvidia has been a "super sticky organization" for years, in part because employees could take part in the company's extraordinary stock run-up. With the company's shares taking a hit, the leadership upheaval could give rivals a fresh opening to recruit some of its most valuable talent. "For the first time ever," employees may be asking, "How much will my equity be worth? How quickly does it come back?" Prosor said. Nvidia's troubles could serve as a learning opportunity for companies that have flattened management structures, said Alexander Kirss, a director analyst in Gartner's HR practice. "No employee is irreplaceable," he said. "That includes the CEO." The latest on Jensen Huang's ouster from Nvidia and what it means for the company's future

title: Nvidia closes below $4T market cap for first time since July 2025 in Huang fallout - CNBC
content:
Nvidia stock sank another 2.01% on Friday, closing below $4 trillion in market cap for the first time since July 2025 as investors navigated the fallout from CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation. Colette Kress, Nvidia’s CFO, will take over as interim CEO, the company announced Thursday. Following the announcement of Huang’s departure, shares of Nvidia declined sharply Thursday morning before recovering to close just 4% lower. The stock declined 12.75% in the trading week, marking its sixth straight weekly decline and its longest such streak since 2012. Huang was under increasing scrutiny after a series of reports that the CEO was in a relationship with a Chinese woman believed to be a spy for Beijing. Huang disclosed that he had an affair on Sunday in a note to employees. The board also announced an investigation into the matter on Sunday. The New York Times reported on Wednesday that Huang had another extramarital romantic relationship, this one with Kimberly Powell, vice president of health care at Nvidia. Reuters reported on Thursday the existence of yet another affair with an Nvidia employee, which the news agency did not name. Nvidia did not immediately respond to CNBC’s request for comment. Before Huang resigned, several Wall Street analysts told CNBC that his departure could cost Nvidia as much as 20% of its market value, given how critical he has been to the company’s success. Nvidia’s stock was already down more than 20% over the last month. Stephane Houri, head of equity research at ODDO BHF, said much of the company’s success has been built around Huang, and his influence extended into the broader industry. Houri told CNBC’s “Squawk Box Europe” on Friday that the architecture of the AI industry “really depended on the vision” and expertise of Huang. — CNBC’s Caleigh Keating contributed to this report. NVIDIA Corporation (NVDA) is facing a new test after co-founder Jensen Huang resigned as chief executive amid a personal-conduct scandal and national-security questions. For shareholders, the immediate issue is whether the leadership shakeup changes the company’s earnings outlook, competitive position or the price investors are willing to pay for its growth. Jonathan Rose isn’t waiting for the dust to settle. During his November 12 Masters in Trading: LIVE, Jonathan said: “I am buying Nvidia right now.” He said he bought shares that morning and was bullish at prevailing prices. Later in the session, he said he had increased his personal position by roughly 20% to 25%. Our analysts aren’t all making the same call, and that’s useful. Jonathan is buying. Louis Navellier is holding and waiting for earnings. Luke Lango is watching how Nvidia’s competitive position evolves, while Eric Fry is asking whether investors will still pay the same premium for its growth. We’ll take a closer look at each of their views, but first, here’s how the scandal unfolded. What started as a personal scandal quickly became a much bigger problem for Nvidia. On November 8, Jensen Huang, Nvidia’s co-founder and longtime CEO, admitted he’d been unfaithful to his wife. According to The New York Times, the woman was Alice Huang (no relation), a Chinese citizen and executive at Singapore-based data center company Megaspeed, an Nvidia customer. U.S. intelligence officials reportedly suspected Alice Huang of gathering information for Beijing. Megaspeed had also faced scrutiny over whether advanced Nvidia chips were being diverted to China in violation of U.S. export restrictions. That raised an uncomfortable question: Could sensitive information have fallen into the wrong hands? Nvidia’s board launched an independent investigation, and Jensen publicly apologized to his family, employees and shareholders. On November 11, The New York Times reported a second alleged relationship, this time with Kimberly Powell, an Nvidia executive who reported to Jensen. By November 12, Jensen had resigned, and longtime Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress had been named interim CEO. To be clear, the allegations involving Chinese intelligence remain unproven publicly, and there’s no established finding that Jensen compromised confidential information. But investors now face a very real question: Can Nvidia maintain its dominance in AI chips without the man who helped build it? The answer depends on more than who occupies the CEO’s office. Nvidia’s earnings power, its competitive position and investor confidence will all help determine what comes next. And as the latest commentary from our analysts Jonathan, Louis, Luke and Eric shows, there are different ways to assess Nvidia’s prospects from here. Jonathan made that distinction in his November 12 Masters in Trading: LIVE. He called the leadership crisis “a Jensen problem,” and he sees the selloff as a buying opportunity. Jonathan’s bullish case rests on the company’s existing business and the market’s reaction. Nvidia’s chips remain deeply embedded in customers’ computing systems, he argued, and changing suppliers takes years. He believes the stock has become inexpensive following the selloff and that investors may be discounting the company too heavily for the uncertainty around its former CEO. His preferred way to express that view is important. Jonathan favors buying Nvidia shares rather than purchasing upside call options ahead of earnings. During the same session, he noted that Nvidia options were pricing in a roughly 12% move around the upcoming earnings report, a level he considered expensive given that the stock had exceeded that threshold only once in its previous 12 earnings reports. Jonathan knows the next earnings report could change the conversation, and he expects earnings and guidance to drive the stock’s next move. Louis isn’t letting the headlines drive his investment decisions. Before Jensen resigned, Louis discussed the unfolding scandal on Market Buzz and initially believed Nvidia’s board and the U.S. government would eventually clear Jensen of wrongdoing. His departure caught Louis by surprise, but it hasn’t shaken his confidence in Nvidia’s underlying business. For Louis, the earnings story still matters more than the headlines. Before the scandal, analysts were forecasting about 91% sales growth and 90% earnings growth for Nvidia’s third quarter. Those were the expectations Louis cited when explaining why he believes the company’s earnings power remains intact. Nvidia still has its technology, its customers and enormous demand for the chips powering the AI boom. But Louis wants to see how the leadership shakeup affects the company’s outlook. He’s particularly interested in Nvidia’s November 17 earnings report, management’s guidance and whether Wall Street analysts begin lowering their estimates. For now, Louis is holding his Nvidia shares, rather than buying more or selling in response to the scandal. There’s another reason he’s being selective. Louis believes the stock market was already rotating away from some of its familiar technology leaders before Jensen’s resignation. He sees opportunities emerging in other sectors, including energy and healthcare, where his quantitative system is identifying companies with strong earnings prospects. His approach comes down to a simple principle: Follow the sales and earnings, not the headlines. Is Nvidia still one of the best stocks to own, or are stronger opportunities emerging elsewhere? Louis follows the earnings to identify stocks with the greatest potential. Get his free stock picks and daily market insights with the Market 360 e-letter. Sign up for free here. Luke expects AI demand to survive Jensen’s exit. His question is how much of that demand Nvidia will capture. Luke has been making the case that the AI trade could broaden beyond Nvidia. He argues that Jensen’s departure may make it easier for major customers to consider other chip suppliers. He sees that as a competitive risk for Nvidia, even as overall AI spending keeps growing. He sees potential openings for Advanced Micro Devices, Inc. (AMD) and custom AI chips, including those supported by Broadcom Inc. (AVGO). Nvidia can remain a major winner in a growing market while facing more competition on price and share. That’s the possibility Luke wants investors to watch. None of that means customers can replace Nvidia overnight. Its installed technology and product roadmap still matter. Luke’s longer-term thesis needs evidence, particularly signs that large buyers are shifting spending to competing platforms. Could Nvidia’s troubles create opportunities elsewhere in AI? Luke follows the companies and technologies that could benefit as the AI market evolves. Get his insights and free stock picks through his Hypergrowth Investing e-letter. Sign up for free. Even if Nvidia keeps delivering strong sales and earnings, its shares could struggle if investors decide to pay a lower multiple for those profits. Eric sees governance questions, regulatory scrutiny and rising competition as possible reasons that confidence could shift. Eric also noted that some competing chip stocks gained during part of Nvidia’s earlier decline. He cautioned that a few days of trading don’t prove Nvidia has lost customers. That would have to show up in orders, spending and earnings. His point is that a great business and a great stock aren’t always the same thing at every price. Is Nvidia’s stock still worth the price? Nvidia (NVDA) stock would likely take a sharp initial hit if CEO Jensen Huang stepped down, but I believe the long-term investment case would remain intact. Huang has led Nvidia since co-founding it in 1993, making his leadership central to the chipmaker's identity and success. Its board is now investigating reports that he was the target of a Chinese intelligence effort. Management has never shared a clear succession plan on who would take over if Huang left, but I'm still bullish on NVDA. The probe hasn't touched the enormous demand for these chips so far, and the stock seems to be priced as if the worst case has happened. As investors and spectators would expect, this probe goes straight to the top. On November 8, the board said a committee of independent directors would run the review with outside counsel. It added that it had no reason to believe that national security or company secrets were compromised. Huang is cooperating and stays on as CEO for now, a welcome update from those who have been following the company closely and appreciate the significant role that Huang has played in the development of the sector, and of course the company. The New York Times reported that U.S. officials believe she was a Chinese intelligence asset, and that Megaspeed bought more than $4.8 billion worth of Nvidia chips over two years. Huang then admitted to a personal relationship with her in a note to staff. Beijing has naturally called the spying claims smears. Of course, this story became highly political almost immediately, and most of Washington isn't letting it go. Three House committee chairs want Huang at a closed-door briefing on November 18, one day after earnings. Committee chair Brian Mast is reportedly weighing a subpoena if Huang says no. House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries has also backed limits on chip sales to China in the annual defense bill. Thinking about all of this as a potential investor, Nvidia has surprisingly never named a successor or explained how it would pick one. Semafor found that the word "succession" doesn't appear once in Nvidia's latest annual report. Microsoft (MSFT) uses it 25 times and Alphabet (GOOGL) uses it 16 times. Huang also has more than 50 people reporting directly to him, so there's no obvious number two to step up, with the exception of some family members perhaps. To me, that's a very deliberate move. Huang has said on occasion that planning around a small, hand-picked group of heirs is toxic, and he'd rather grow a wider group of leaders across the company. Asked in January 2026 how long he'd stay, his answer was "for as long as I deserve it." It's worked pretty well so far for shareholders. However, it also leaves the board without a ready answer if it suddenly needs one. Some analysts are now putting a number on that gap. Analyst Dan Ives of Yorkville Ives said Nvidia would be worth 25% to 30% less if Huang were removed. Bernstein downgraded the stock to Outperform with a $200 price target. The names floated as potential stand-ins, such as CFO Colette Kress and co-founder Chris Malachowsky, come from media speculation, not from anything the board has actually said. These feel like safe hands to me, but the sheer power of leadership Huang has demonstrated would be almost impossible to match. Meanwhile, the business momentum Nvidia carried into the fall remains hard to ignore. Q2 Fiscal 2027 revenue rose 106% year-over-year to $96.2 billion. Data center sales climbed 117% to $89 billion, and gross margins held at 75%. For Q3, management guided to about $108 billion in revenue, give or take 2%. That outlook notably assumes zero data center compute sales to China. CFO Colette Kress has also said she expects 70% revenue growth in FY28. If Nvidia hits its guide on November 17, the conversation should shift back to demand, at least for a while. Wednesday gave a hint of that. Shares jumped about 5% in early trading after AI cloud provider CoreWeave (CRWV) raised its outlook, which is a reminder that Nvidia's biggest customers are still spending. Even so, the stock is still down about 15% in November. Much of the slide started before the probe, with the stock losing roughly 22% to 24% from its early-October peak through the post-midterm chip sell-off. I would tend to think that a fair amount of the leadership risk is already baked in after such a heavy news event. Nvidia trades at about 21x trailing earnings. On a forward basis, some analysts put the stock at 18.65x. The semiconductor industry's median forward P/E is close to 20.31x, so Nvidia trades at a modest discount of roughly 8% to its peers. Against its own history, the gap is much wider. At 18.65x, the stock is valued at less than half its five-year average of 41.38x, even after more than doubling its sales last quarter. So what's the company worth without its charismatic CEO? At 18.65x, the market is assuming forward earnings of about $9.32 per share. Some analysts speculate that Nvidia without Huang might trade at 10x to 12x, which, by my calculations, comes to roughly $93 to $112. Knock 25% to 30% off today's price, as Ives suggests, and you land at roughly $122 to $130, which is a milder downside than the multiple-compression case. If the board clears Huang and the multiple drifts back toward the sector median of 20.31x, the numbers point to around $189. I'd take that trade, as long as earnings estimates hold up. However, not everyone agrees: Baird cut NVDA to Hold with a $200 target on November 11, and Citi (C) trimmed its target to $225. Wall Street is still firmly behind Nvidia, though the support has thinned slightly this week. NVDA has a Strong Buy consensus based on 29 Buys and seven Holds over the past three months. The average NVDA price target of $290.90 implies 67.44% upside from the last price. For 33 years, Nvidia and Huang have been almost synonymous, and this probe makes it understandable for investors to picture one without the other. With no clear successor, I'd expect a pretty sharp drop if he were forced out. However, the business itself still looks strong, and the shares already trade well below their own history and the sector. Bitcoin investors have nobody, and that may be the biggest difference between the two assets. But here's the catch: Wall Street has poured billions into Bitcoin ETF products, which were originally designed to operate without a corporate leader. NVDA stock, meanwhile, carries a CEO premium built around Huang's influence over AI. Nvidia shares plunged more than 8% in after-hours trading today, after its board considered Huang's future. The move threatened to erase around $600 billion in market value. Chip demand had not suddenly disappeared. Investor confidence in Nvidia's leader had become the driver. Huang is more than Nvidia's chief executive. He is its chief strategist and public evangelist for the AI boom. Reuters reported that more than 60 executives report directly to him, while analysts see no obvious successor who could replace his influence seamlessly. That concentration creates upside when investors trust the leader. Huang can turn a keynote or forecast into a market-moving event. It also creates vulnerability: investors struggle to separate the person from the company. NVDA stock still symbolizes ownership of chips central to AI infrastructure. Yet reports of a possible leadership change were enough to shake the stock and its partners. It's a CEO premium phenomenon, the confidence investors attach to one individual. Apple offers a historical comparison. When Steve Jobs resigned as CEO on August 24, 2011, Apple shares fell 5.9% in after-hours trading. Tim Cook took over, and the company continued to grow. Apple shares have since climbed 1,946% during Cook's tenure. But what's the difference? Apple had succession planning and an operating business. Bitcoin was built around a different proposition. Satoshi Nakamoto disappeared from public view years ago. Bitcoin kept running. There is no CEO to reassure holders, no board to appoint a successor, and no quarterly call where a founder promises a better product cycle. Its issuance schedule and consensus rules do not depend on a personality. But Bitcoin is not immune to sentiment. Its price still responds to adoption, regulation, security, liquidity, and demand. But its sentiment is less dependent on a single executive. Nobody has to decide whether Satoshi is still the right person for the job. The Bitcoin ETF market shows how much Wall Street has changed the ownership story. US spot Bitcoin ETFs have attracted $55.4 billion in cumulative net inflows since launching in January 2024. The funds held about 1.31 million BTC on November 11, equal to 6.5% of Bitcoin's 20.11 million current circulating supply. BlackRock's IBIT alone held about 793,069 BTC on November 9, worth nearly $59.5 billion. It offers traditional portfolios Bitcoin exposure without wallet or private-key management. This is the Bitcoin ETF Paradox. Wall Street does not control Bitcoin's protocol, but its products now shape a huge part of the market's demand narrative. Inflows can strengthen buying pressure. Redemptions can reverse it. Investors increasingly watch BlackRock and Fidelity flows for clues about institutional appetite. A world without ETFs would look different. The $55.4 billion in net inflows would not have entered through these products. Some investors might have bought Bitcoin directly, used futures, or stayed away. The funds' 1.31 million BTC would have had different owners, and the market would have lost a major regulated route for institutional access. Subtracting $55.4 billion from Bitcoin's market value would not reveal its ETF-free price. Market capitalization is set by marginal trades, not by adding every dollar invested. The real counterfactual concerns demand, access, and who is willing to buy when prices fall. That is where Bitcoin's advantage and its new weakness meet. Nvidia's CEO premium can become a liability when confidence in Jensen Huang cracks. Bitcoin has no founder to lose. Bitcoin never needed Satoshi to keep the network alive. Wall Street, however, has taught a new generation of buyers to watch its flows. The protocol remains decentralized. The investment narrative is increasingly institutional. title: ‘A dark day for Nvidia’: Here’s what analysts have been saying about Jensen Huang’s departure - CNBC
content:
Nvidia investors are preparing for a future without Jensen Huang after the CEO’s resignation was announced on Thursday. Markets were on tenterhooks ahead of the decision amid reports that the chip giant’s board had convened to discuss his future with the company. By the time of the announcement, at least six analysts had downgraded the stock between Wednesday night and Thursday morning. The New York Times on Wednesday reported that Huang had engaged in a second extramarital affair with an employee. The CEO was already under scrutiny after Huang admitted to having a romantic relationship with a woman U.S. intelligence believes is a Chinese spy. Nvidia announced on Thursday morning that, following a board meeting, Huang would step down after more than 30 years at the company’s helm. Those downgrading the stock included longtime Nvidia bull Ben Reitzes of Melius Research. Nvidia shares were seen down more than 12% shortly after the open on Wall Street, bringing losses for the last month close to 25%. Here’s what analysts and investors are saying about the company and the stock. Reitzes changed his rating for Nvidia to hold from buy. His price target is now $185 — down from $315 — is 6% above the level at which shares last closed. “We thought we had experience, but nothing prepares you for what has happened at Nvidia over the last few weeks - and especially since Saturday. The only situation remotely close to this we can recall was HP in 2010. Waiting to see what that Board would do (and who they would hire) that time didn’t work out. It was really cheap, too, at ~9x EPS right after its initial swoon. Nvidia is a much stronger, more important company, but its market moves far faster, and this story touches geopolitical flashpoints. In this unique crisis, we have decided (reluctantly) to step aside on Nvidia (now a Hold) after recommending it since we launched our AI platform coverage universe in July 2023,” he said. Analyst Mark Lipacis downgraded Nvidia to in line from outperform. He also lowered his price target on shares to $186 from $465, implying 7% upside from Wednesday’s close. “The Wall Street Journal reported Nvidia’s Board was ‘preparing to oust’ its CEO after he had two extramarital affairs, including one with a suspected Chinese spy. The NY Times reported that Nvidia’s Board hired law firm Wachtell Lipton to lead an investigation into the matter. While Nvidia’s Board said that it ‘has no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised,’ we believe that the investigation will take time and we expect NVDA’s P/E multiple will continue to compress consistent with our ‘Late-Innings of the Semi Cycle’ thesis, especially since Nvidia has no obvious succession plan or number 2 operational executive,” he said. William Blair’s Sebastien Naji downgraded Nvidia to market perform from outperform. “After a head-spinning week of news and allegations around CEO Jensen Huang, Nvidia’s board is reportedly preparing to remove him, according to the Wall Street Journal. The full story will take time to emerge and may require several investigations, including the board’s own independent probe and a requested U.S. House briefing. What is already clear is that Huang’s likely departure and heightened scrutiny of the company will be a significant overhang on NVDA shares in the near term. Meanwhile, the potential for a slower AI buildout and more intense competition from other chipmakers will only add to execution risk...governance and regulatory pressure, the potential for more serious fallout, and a sudden change in management are likely to muddle both execution and sentiment. As a result, we are downgrading NVDA to Market Perform and will wait for the dust to settle before reassessing,” he said. Analyst Rick Schafer downgraded the AI stock to perform from outperform. “We are downgrading shares of NVDA and removing our price target following reports (WSJ, NYT) of founding CEO Jensen Huang’s imminent departure amidst allegations of a 2nd extramarital affair. Credible media reports circulated Wednesday evening that NVDA’s board is preparing to part ways with Huang following a widely reported relationship with an alleged Chinese spy compounded by new allegations of a relationship with an NVDA executive. This ‘one-two’ punch appears to have forced the board’s hand...While we see upside to the F3Q (Oct.) print and F4Q (Jan.) outlook, we expect fundamentals to take a backseat near term. The departure of Mr. Huang could, in our view, translate to a lingering share overhang,” he said. Analyst Stacy Rasgon slashed his price target from $400 and downgraded the stock from market outperform. “So now what? On the positive, the fundamentals of the business (if not the leadership) areclearly still intact with numbers that remain massive (and probably still headed higher). We don’t think the company should have huge issues operating while engaged in a search for new leadership. And (of course) the shares are almost absurdly cheap (and getting cheaper as we speak); clearly there is a lot of bad news getting priced in here,” he said. “On the other hand, we find it hard to advocate stepping in here in size as there will no doubt be more allegations to come (there is a trope that says if you find two ants in your kitchen the best estimate of the total number of ants in your kitchen is not two...), both from internal issues as well as headlines related to the business, new governmental investigations etc. Adding on the new variable of who will take the reins (internal? external?) and anything else they may or may not uncover creates additional uncertainty (and we can’t even begin to speculate as to who they might find to fill Jensen’s shoes),” he added. Analyst John Vinh downgraded the stock from overweight. “We believe Huang’s departure represents a material increase in strategic, organizational, and execution risk that warrants a higher risk premium and lower valuation multiple for the stock. While we expect core fundamentals to remain strong for the foreseeable future, we believe it will be challenging for NVDA to find a successor with the same leadership and strategic vision as Huang,” he said. “In our view the writing is on the wall that Jensen’s days at Nvidia could be numbered and we would expect this to be a very fluid situation over the next 48 hours,” renowned tech bull Dan Ives said in a note overnight. “Jensen has created a black eye moment for himself and Nvidia and now has created a spider web of complexity that Wall Street, Silicon Valley, DC, and the global tech ecosystem are trying to figure out what is next.” “We believe Nvidia’s value is $300 per share with Jensen as CEO and $225 per share without Jensen as CEO,” Ives added. “The stock will clearly be under pressure with this fluid news but the reality is its a dark day for Nvidia, but the company will navigate this turmoil and get through to the other side and remain a core foundational piece of the AI Revolution.” Citi analysts said overnight that they had trimmed their target price for Nvidia to $225, down from $285. “If Jensen were forced out, it would mark the end of an era,” Malik and Sylla said in their note. “Under his leadership, Nvidia became the dominant force in AI infrastructure, the primary beneficiary of the global AI spending cycle, and one of the world’s most valuable companies. A leadership transition creates an overhang on the stock given his central role in strategy, product vision, customer relationships, and investor confidence.” They said Nvidia CFO Colette Kress could serve as interim CEO while the board evaluates external candidates. “As much as there is a lesson here for Nvidia around corporate governance, around key man risk… the reality is there is still 40,000 other employees at Nvidia, and there is some real talent there, and I have no doubt that there are some executors within Nvidia that the board will be able to tap to execute on their existing plans and continue to manage the company,” Nathan Thooft, the firm’s CIO, told CNBC’s “Squawk Box Asia” on Thursday. “I think the bigger risk is the foresight in the next several years, where Nvidia was driven by a lot of the mindset and thoughts that come out of their CEO, and if he’s no longer there they’re going to have to find that replacement.” “You can’t deny the board has done a horrible job of succession planning,” Greifeld told CNBC’s “Morning Call” on Thursday. “What the board has to find out in the next days or weeks is, did Jensen lie to them? Right? Did he lie to them repeatedly on different topics? We don’t know. Does he lose their trust basically on lying to them over the years? I’m sure the board would love to keep Jensen in place in some role. Right, his value to the company is quite large.” Greifeld said he does not see a premium in Nvidia stock, noting that it trades at a low multiple “so there’s no bubble to burst here with respect to the valuation.” “If there’s a new CEO in, they don’t have to make any decisions day one, day 30, day 60. They have time to really get their footing and come up with their own strategic vision,” he told CNBC. “You’re not going to change what is in the development plan for chips that exists today. So I think certainly it would be a loss, but given the nature of the business and the long lead time for these chip developments and the long contractual relationships they have with customers, it would give them certainly room to maneuver.” CIO Richard Reyle told CNBC’s “Squawk Box Asia” that Nvidia’s board had painted themselves into a corner by not having any kind of succession plan in place. “I’ve heard him compared to Steve Jobs being removed from Apple, but [Jobs] put in place a succession plan and cultivated and groomed Tim Cook for years, so that when he passed away and [Cook] took over, there was a real leader there,” he said. “Right now, Nvidia doesn’t have that person in place, so it’s going to be a choice of keeping Jensen and being faced with … all kinds of interrogations, or they’re going to have to move on from him, and that’s just going to make the stock uninvestable. That doesn’t make the AI trade uninvestable, but it certainly makes Nvidia uninvestable.” Reyle said he saw the stock moving “lower and much lower from here.” “There’s no obvious [replacement] there that can step right in and take over, so they may kind of try to ride this out and retain him,” he said. “But there’s going to be a lot of difficulty in doing so because he’s going to become something of a liability.” “NVIDIA upheaval puts tech concentration risks in focus,” Mark Haefele, global wealth management chief investment officer at UBS, and his team said on Thursday morning. “Without taking any views on individual companies, the episode reinforces the importance of investment diversification and selectivity as the AI trade matures. We retain our conviction in AI’s long-term potential, with compute demand remaining robust and earnings resilient. But elevated expectations and potentially wide differences in company outcomes can leave concentrated portfolios exposed to company-specific setbacks.” “Jensen Huang is toast,” Bill Blain, founder and principal, said in his morning newsletter. “Nvidia’s dependence on Jensen Huang is now exposed as a major market risk. The dominant firm within the AI industry lacks clear succession planning and Huang was seen as the acceptable face of AI by the public.” “Confidence in the AI sector has been wobbling for months,” he added. “Huang’s departure could lead to instability and trigger another collapse.” Got a confidential news tip? title: Nvidia stock closes down over 4% after CEO Jensen Huang announces resignation - CNBC
content:
Follow CNBC’s live coverage of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation here. Nvidia shares declined 4.34% Thursday after Jensen Huang announced he would immediately step down as CEO and a member of the board at the chipmaker. The stock hovered under $4 trillion in market cap for most of the day, but climbed slightly heading into the close to finish above the number. The 4% fall pared steeper losses earlier in the day of as much as 14%. Nvidia has closed above the $4 trillion market cap benchmark since July 2025. Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress will serve as interim CEO until a new leader is appointed, Nvidia said in a Thursday statement. Harvey C. Jones, former CEO of Synopsys, will become the first-ever chair of the board. On Sunday, Huang admitted to having an affair. The CEO was romantically involved with Alice Huang, an executive at cloud company Megaspeed, according to The Financial Times, who U.S. intelligence officials believe is a spy for China. Alice Huang is also tied to Nvidia’s biggest competitor in China, Huawei, and may have owned stakes in Chinese businesses benefitting Huawei while simultaneously doing business with Nvidia, CNBC’s Eamon Javers exclusively reported Thursday. The New York Times on Wednesday reported that Huang had another extramarital relationship with Kimberly Powell, vice president of health care at Nvidia. Powell reports to Huang, according to the Times. Huang also had an “intimate relationship” with an unnamed second employee, Reuters reported Thursday. Before Huang resigned, several Wall Street analysts told CNBC that this departure could lead the stock to fall 20%, given how critical he has been to Nvidia’s success. Nvidia’s stock is already down more than 20% over the last month. Bernstein on Thursday slashed its price target on Nvidia’s stock by half from $400 to $200. Stacy Rasgon, a senior analyst at Bernstein, told CNBC’s “Squawk Box Asia” on Thursday that Huang’s alleged affair with a direct report means it is “much tougher for the board to leave him in position.” Huang was central to Nvidia’s rise, having co-founded the company in 1993 and was pivotal in transforming Nvidia from a gaming hardware player to the company at the center of the artificial intelligence boom. Rasgon said it is unclear who could be the “visionary” to lead Nvidia into the future as new CEO. “Jensen is Nvidia, right? He is the visionary. The reason they’re in the position that they’re in today is because he made decisions 10 years ago,” Rasgon said. “Who is the right person now to make the decisions for the next 10 years? I don’t intuitively know who that person would be.” Earlier, U.S. lawmakers had called for Huang’s resignation, adding further pressure to the CEO and the company. Richard Reyle, chief investment officer at Questar Capital Partners, said Nvidia’s lack of a succession plan makes the stock “uninvestable.” “Nvidia doesn’t have that person in place, and so it’s going to be either a choice of keeping Jensen and being faced with months and months of being hauled in front of probably congressional boards and things to explain themselves and all kinds of interrogations,” Reyle told CNBC’s “Access Middle East.” “Or they’re going to have to move on from him, and that’s just going to make the stock uninvestable. That doesn’t make the AI trade uninvestable, but it certainly makes Nvidia uninvestable.” Got a confidential news tip? We want to hear from you.
